Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Cold Temperature: Cold, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Lina, a 42-year-old project manager, had always prided herself on her meticulous planning and unwavering focus, qualities that served her well in her demanding career and her marriage. But a year and a half ago, her world was violently upended by a sudden, severe bout of pneumonia that quickly escalated into sepsis, leaving her fighting for her life in the intensive care unit. She remembered flashes: the piercing cold of the hospital room, the acrid, metallic tang of the air, the constant visual presence of IV drips and monitors, a blur of needles and tubes. The memory of that time was profoundly unsettling; some moments, like the chilling sensation of the ventilator tube in her throat, were terrifyingly vivid, yet the overall experience felt surreal, as if it had happened to someone else entirely. Often, a wave of profound despair or terror would wash over her, a visceral emotional intensity, without any accompanying image or clear recollection of what precisely triggered the feeling.

Since then, Lina’s life had become a careful navigation of a landscape fraught with hidden dangers. Her office, a modern building with powerful air conditioning, was a constant challenge. The slightest chill in the air would send a jolt of panic through her, reminding her of the pervasive cold of the ICU. Similarly, certain smells – the sterile scent of cleaning products, or even the faint aroma of a particular hospital-grade hand sanitizer someone used – could instantly transport her back to the ward, triggering a cascade of internal distress. Even seeing medical equipment on television, or a discarded syringe wrapper in the street, would make her heart pound, a reminder of the vulnerability she had experienced.

She found herself engaged in an exhausting internal battle. She tried desperately to erase the memory of the event, pushing it away with all her might whenever a fragment surfaced. This constant mental effort was draining, yet it felt essential. What frightened her most was the creeping suspicion that she was losing her mind, so she constantly monitored her own thoughts, searching for any sign of irrationality or impending breakdown. A deep certainty had settled within her: her body had been permanently damaged by what happened, leaving her fragile and susceptible. She also believed, with a heavy heart, that her life as she knew it had been destroyed, and that she had failed in her most important role, both as a competent professional and as a supportive partner to her husband, who now often looked at her with a worried, pitying gaze she couldn't stand.

This fear and self-reproach translated into concrete changes in her daily existence. She began to avoid medical settings entirely, cancelling her annual physical examination and finding excuses to skip routine dental check-ups, terrified of encountering a needle or the clinical scent of a doctor’s office. Her husband’s gentle suggestions to seek follow-up care for her lingering fatigue were met with sharp, uncharacteristic resistance. At work, her once-sharp focus was now fractured. She struggled to concentrate in meetings if the air conditioning was too high, or if a colleague wore a perfume that vaguely resembled a hospital disinfectant. She had started making excuses to work from home more often, isolating herself and her growing anxieties. This withdrawal had started to impact her project deadlines and her team's morale, leaving her feeling increasingly ineffective and reinforcing her appraisal that she was failing. The once vibrant woman, known for her calm competence, was now a shadow of her former self, constantly on edge, haunted by an invisible past. It was the growing distance she felt from her husband, and the realization that her work performance was slipping irrevocably, that finally compelled Lina to seek help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the life she felt had been stolen from her.
